body.objective: Students will be able to tell beat from rhythm.
body.iCan: I can tell beat from rhythm.
successCriteria: I can tell the difference between beat and rhythm

body.hook: Put your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. It's steady: thump, thump, thump. Now say your full name out loud and clap each syllable. That pattern is different from your heartbeat. The steady pulse is the beat; the pattern of sounds is the rhythm. Every song you know is built from both.

study.title: Beat vs Rhythm
study.question: How do beat and rhythm work together?
study.passage:
Part 1, Feel the beat (5 minutes): The teacher plays a recording of a song with a clear steady beat (for example, a pop or folk song at about 100 beats per minute). Students tap the beat on their knees. Then half the class keeps the beat while the other half claps the rhythm of the melody or lyrics.
Part 2, Rhythm syllables (10 minutes): Learn counting for 4/4 time:
• Quarter note = "ta" = 1 beat (count "1")
• Two eighth notes = "ti-ti" = 1 beat (count "1-and")
• Half note = "ta-a" = 2 beats
• Whole note = "ta-a-a-a" = 4 beats
• Quarter rest = silence for 1 beat
Practise reading rhythm cards:
Card A: ta ta ti-ti ta
Card B: ta-a ta ta
Card C: ti-ti ti-ti ta (rest)
Card D: ta-a-a-a
Part 3, Name rhythms (5 minutes): Clap the rhythm of your name, then a food (for example, "pizza" = ti-ti, "macaroni" = ti-ti ti-ti).
Part 4, Create (10 minutes): In pairs, write a four-beat rhythm using at least three note values, and perform it on a drum or by clapping while the class keeps the beat.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.hook: Every song you've ever heard is built from sounds of different lengths. Music notation is a code that tells performers exactly how long each sound lasts. Once you crack it, you can read rhythms you've never heard before.

study.title: Crack the Rhythm Code
study.question: How do note values tell us how long sounds last?
study.passage:
Rhythm chart (written for this lesson, in 4/4 time):
Whole note (open oval, no stem) = 4 beats; count "1-2-3-4." Whole rest = a block hanging below a line.
Half note (open oval with stem) = 2 beats; count "1-2." Half rest = a block sitting on a line.
Quarter note (filled oval with stem) = 1 beat; count "1." Quarter rest = a squiggle.
Eighth notes (filled ovals with flags or a beam) = ½ beat each; count "1-and." Eighth rest = a small "7" shape.
Activities: 1. Note-value pizza: one whole note = 2 halves = 4 quarters = 8 eighths. 2. Echo clapping: the teacher claps four beats; the class echoes. 3. Read and clap four rhythm cards, counting aloud ("1 2-and 3 4"). 4. Rests: show silence with open hands. 5. Write a four-bar rhythm using each note value at least once, then swap with a partner to clap.

body.objective: Students will be able to identify time signatures.
successCriteria: I can explain what the top and bottom numbers of a time signature mean

body.hook: Stand up and march: LEFT-right, LEFT-right. Now waltz: ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three. You already feel time signatures in your body. The numbers at the start of the music just write that feeling down.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers at the start of music showing beats per bar and which note gets the beat.
The pattern of strong and weak beats.
A section of music between two bar lines.
A vertical line that divides music into bars.
The first, strongest beat of a bar.

study.title: Feel the Metre
study.question: How do time signatures organize the beat?
study.passage:
Time signatures (written for this lesson):
Top number = how many beats in each bar. Bottom number = which note gets one beat (4 = quarter note).
2/4: two beats per bar, STRONG-weak, like a march. Conduct: down, up.
3/4: three beats per bar, STRONG-weak-weak, like a waltz. Conduct: down, out, up (a triangle).
4/4: four beats per bar, STRONG-weak-medium-weak, the most common metre in pop music. Conduct: down, in, out, up.
Listening task: Listen to short excerpts and decide the metre by finding the strong beat and counting:
1. A military march (2/4). 2. Johann Strauss II, The Blue Danube waltz (1866) (3/4). 3. A pop song (4/4). 4. "Happy Birthday" (3/4).
Then conduct along with each excerpt.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers play excerpts from public recordings.
